standard.title: Punctuation for referencing and citing
standard.description: understand punctuation conventions for referencing and citing others for formal and informal purposes
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how colons and brackets support meaning (AC9E7LA09). They have not yet examined the punctuation conventions specific to referencing and citation — how to integrate others' words and ideas into their own writing with appropriate attribution.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students understand punctuation conventions for referencing and citing others in formal and informal contexts, including when to use direct quotation and when to report sources.

nodes.label: Direct quotation conventions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply punctuation conventions for integrating direct quotations into their own writing.
nodes.minimum_width: Apply correct punctuation for at least two direct quotations in a piece of writing, including quotation marks, attribution and any necessary punctuation for integration.
nodes.typical_width: Apply punctuation conventions for direct quotations across a range of integration contexts — introducing, interrupting and following up quotations in essays, reviews and academic assignments.
wider: Compare how different citation conventions (e.g. APA, MLA, Chicago) handle the punctuation of direct quotation, and explain why standardisation matters in academic contexts
Examine how journalistic quotation conventions differ from academic ones, and what this reveals about different relationships to source attribution

response_modes.reason: Quotation punctuation is a precision skill — students know the rules in isolation but errors accumulate under compositional pressure. Practice embedding quotations in their own writing matters more here than conceptual breadth.

success_criteria: Student correctly punctuates direct quotations including quotation marks and integration punctuation
Student attributes quotations to their source appropriately
nodes.hinge_reason: Quotation punctuation errors are systemic in formal writing tasks — students who haven't secured the conventions at N1 produce incorrectly formatted citations throughout their assessed analytical writing.

nodes.label: When to quote vs paraphrase or report
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain when direct quotation is appropriate versus paraphrasing or general source reporting, and apply this judgment in their writing.
nodes.minimum_width: Make and justify one decision to use a direct quotation and one decision to paraphrase or report a source, explaining the reasoning for each choice.
nodes.typical_width: Apply and explain decisions about quoting directly versus paraphrasing or reporting sources across a formal writing task, justifying each attribution choice based on purpose and context.
wider: Analyse how over-quoting weakens an argument in student essays, and develop principles for deciding when the author's exact words add value vs when paraphrase serves better
Compare attribution practices in academic writing versus opinion writing, and examine what different conventions reveal about the relationship between writer and source

response_modes.reason: The judgment about when to quote directly requires explicit reasoning criteria that students rarely develop spontaneously. A scaffold (does the exact wording matter? is the authority of the source relevant? does paraphrase lose something important?) helps students make principled rather than habitual decisions.

success_criteria: Student makes an attribution choice (quote vs paraphrase) and can explain the reasoning
Student's written attribution correctly signals the relationship between their own ideas and the source
